key_insight: Distributionally Robust Schrödinger Bridge (DRSB) learns a single stochastic transport controller that remains effective even when the test-time initial distribution shifts.
engineering_relevance: This makes learned transport more reliable for deployment in uncertain or perturbed input conditions, at the cost of some nominal-performance tradeoff.
method: Formulate a worst-case Schrödinger bridge objective over an ambiguity set of initial distributions.
Combine control energy with a KL penalty between terminal and target distributions.
Use an alternating algorithm to update the adversarial initial distribution, estimate terminal log-density ratios, and train the controller; provide Wasserstein and Sinkhorn gradient variants.
evidence_signal: Experiments on 2D transport tasks, image-to-image translation, and Gaussian mixture transport show improved robustness to input perturbations, with Sinkhorn DRSB achieving lower mean sliced Wasserstein distance than fixed-level noise augmentation at two unseen noise levels.
watch_item: Robustness gains come with reduced nominal performance, and the adversarial-gradient approximations add implementation complexity.
